section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > abstract
text: An organic additive, Diazine Black (DB), was employed as a leveler for microvia filling using copper electroplating. DB is a derivative of Janus Green B (JGB), which is a common leveler used for copper fill of submicron or micron circuit metallization in electronic products. This study determined the optimal DB concentration for achieving the best filling performance. The electrochemical behavior of DB and its interaction with other additives, such as a suppressor and an accelerator were characterized using galvanostatic measurements.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > abstract
text: The electrochemical behavior of DB and its interaction with other additives, such as a suppressor and an accelerator were characterized using galvanostatic measurements. These electrochemical analyses helped explaining the filling mechanism of the plating formula containing the DB. Various surface morphologies and the crystalline orientation of the plated copper films caused by different DB concentrations were characterized by a scanning electron microscope (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD), respectively.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > abstract
text: Various surface morphologies and the crystalline orientation of the plated copper films caused by different DB concentrations were characterized by a scanning electron microscope (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD), respectively. section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 1. Introduction
text: Recently, multifunction and portable electronic products have become part of the mainstream of consumer electronic products. Not only the motherboard of electronic products but also the packaging substrates of integrated circuit (IC) chips need a high-density interconnection (HDI) made by a process using stacked microvias [1,2]. For example, the motherboard of cellular phones uses HDI to integrate more functions.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 1. Introduction
text: For example, the motherboard of cellular phones uses HDI to integrate more functions. Because the diameter of the microvia has shrunk to less than 65 -m, and even as low as 50 -m, several metallization technologies such as filling with resin and conductive paste have not met the demands of process integration [1,2]. Instead, researchers believe that a more promising technology is to fill microvia using copper electroplating because this filling technique has been employed successfully to fabricate the interconnections of IC chips, such as via and trench metallization [3–13].

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 1. Introduction
text: The microvia filling technology using copper electroplating is implemented using a specific plating formula that contains a suppressor, an accelerator, and a leveler [14–17]. The suppressor and the accelerator are basic additives for the microvia filling; the addition of a leveler can significantly improve the filling yield and extend the operative range of the accelerator concentration [16,17]. Janus Green B (JGB) is a familiar leveler that bears one quaternary ammonium cation and one chloride ion.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 1. Introduction
text: Janus Green B (JGB) is a familiar leveler that bears one quaternary ammonium cation and one chloride ion. It preferentially adsorbs at the protrusion to inhibit the copper deposition rate because of the selective adsorption of the quaternary ammonium cation [18]. Therefore, a proper addition of JGB results in a copper deposit with a mirror-like surface. It is an effective reagent for carrying out a void-free filling in dual damascene metallization [4,5,7,8,10]. In addition, JGB can interact with polyethylene glycol (PEG) to form a composite suppressor whose adsorptive behavior is strongly convection dependent [16,17].

Hence, the addition of JGB can significantly enhance the filling performance of a plating formula because the forced convection acting on the board surface is always stronger than that at the bottom of the microvia during electroplating [20,21].

The behavior of the convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) of a plating formula has been demonstrated to be an indicator that can determine whether the plating formula is a good candidate or not for the microvia filling [17,22,23].

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 1. Introduction
text: The behavior of the convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) of a plating formula has been demonstrated to be an indicator that can determine whether the plating formula is a good candidate or not for the microvia filling [17,22,23]. Recently, many new levelers have been evaluated to determine their effectiveness as additives to copper electroplating for submicron via filling [11–13,24]. These new levelers also have the quaternary ammonium cations, except for polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) [13].

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 1. Introduction
text: These new levelers also have the quaternary ammonium cations, except for polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) [13]. A preliminary evaluation of filling performance using the CDA metrology has shown that the derivative of JGB, namely, Diazine Black (DB), can compete with JGB in filling performance [17]. However, except for a patent [25] which claimed that DB is an effective leveler for copper fill, no detailed research has been undertaken to study DB as a leveler for the microvia filling.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 1. Introduction
text: However, except for a patent [25] which claimed that DB is an effective leveler for copper fill, no detailed research has been undertaken to study DB as a leveler for the microvia filling. Therefore, in this study, we investigated the use of DB as a leveler, including the filling performance of the plating formula, the chemical interactions among the additives, the surface morphology of the copper deposit, and the influence of DB on the crystalline structure. In PCB fabrication, the etching process for patterning circuits is a subsequent step after copper plating.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 2.1. Electroplating
text: The electroplating conditions, procedures, and pretreatment methods have been detailed elsewhere [16,17]. PCB fragments with microvias formed by CO _2 laser ablation were used as test samples for filling plating. The size of the PCB fragment was 1 0 × 6 cm ^2 The via density was 500 in array of 2 0 × 2 5. The distance between two microvias was 220μm or 320μm (from center to center), depending on the diameter of the microvia. The specification of the microvias was described in the caption of cross-section images of these microvias.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 2.1. Electroplating
text: The specification of the microvias was described in the caption of cross-section images of these microvias. Before metallization, the microvias were conducted through a so-called desmear process to remove the smear that was formed by laser ablation on the microvia bottom. The desmear process can thoroughly clean copper surface of the via bottom to make sure of good conductivity at the interface between the filled copper and the inner copper pad after plating. Following the desmear process, electroless copper plating was used for sidewall metallization of the microvia.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 2.1. Electroplating
text: Following the desmear process, electroless copper plating was used for sidewall metallization of the microvia. Following that, a plated copper layer with a thickness of ^2 - 3 -m was deposited on the sidewall to increase the thickness of the copper seed layer for the prevention of oxidation. The PCB fragment was plated at a current density of 1 9.4 mAcm ^- 2 for 70 min. Two phosphorus-containing copper slices were used as anodes and directly placed in the plating bath with a working volume of 1500 mL.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 2.1. Electroplating
text: Two phosphorus-containing copper slices were used as anodes and directly placed in the plating bath with a working volume of 1500 mL. Constant agitation was performed by continuous air bubble flow with a flow rate of 2.5 Lh ^- 1 during electroplating. The composition of the base electrolyte used for all plating tests was 0.88 M CuSO_4 (Riedel-de Haën, ACS) and 0.54 MH_2S0_4 (Merck, 96%, Ultrapure). The additives used herein were PEG with a molecular weight of 8000 (Fluka), NaCl (Fisher, Certified ACS), bis(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) (Raschig GmbH, Germany), and DB (Aldrich).

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 2.1. Electroplating
text: The additives used herein were PEG with a molecular weight of 8000 (Fluka), NaCl (Fisher, Certified ACS), bis(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) (Raschig GmbH, Germany), and DB (Aldrich). They were individually added to the plating bath through dilution from stock solutions that were prepared with properly concentrated contents. The temperature ofthe plating solution was maintained at 25^°C The filling performance of a plating formula was examined through an image of the microvia cross-section obtained from an optical microscope (OM) (Olympus BX51).

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 2.2. Electrochemical analyses
text: The electrochemical characteristics and interaction of various additives were characterized by galvanostatic measurements (GMs) using a PGSTAT30 (Auto-Lab) potentiostat with a three-electrode cell. The base electrolyte formulated for the GM was the same as that ofplating ( i.e.,0.88MCuSO_4. and 0.5 4 M H _ 2 S 0 _ 4). The volume of the tested electrolyte was 100 mL and the temperature of the electrolyte was maintained at 2 5 ^ ° C during analysis. A 3-mm-diameter platinum rotating disk electrode (Pt-RDE) was employed as a base of WE.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 2.2. Electrochemical analyses
text: A 3-mm-diameter platinum rotating disk electrode (Pt-RDE) was employed as a base of WE. Before each electrochemical analysis, a thin copper layer with a thickness of 500 nm was predeposited onto the Pt-RDE in a predeposition bath, which only contained 0.88 M CuSO_4 and 0.54 M H _ 2 S O _ 4, to prepare a Cu-RDE. The counter electrode (CE) was a small copper bar, which was placed in a small glass tube containing the base electrolyte.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 2.2. Electrochemical analyses
text: The counter electrode (CE) was a small copper bar, which was placed in a small glass tube containing the base electrolyte. The end of the small glass tube was sealed with a porous material to prevent direct contact of the additives with the CE during analysis, which in turn produced certain byproducts. A saturated mercurous sulfate electrode (SMSE) served as a reference electrode (RE). The GM of the additive injection was performed using the Cu-RDE at a current density of 19.4 mA cm− 2. At the beginning of the GM, the glass vessel contained only the base electrolyte.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 2.2. Electrochemical analyses
text: At the beginning of the GM, the glass vessel contained only the base electrolyte. After the GM was performed for a period, one additive with a given content was injected into the glass vessel to achieve the desired concentration. The potential variation ofthe Cu-RDE could clearly indicate the electrochemical effect of these additives on copper deposition. The GM was carried out twice. One was carried out using the Cu-RDE at 100 rpm, and the other was carried out at 1000 rpm. A potential difference, Δ η, defined by Δ η = η (average at 100 rpm)  (average at 1000 rpm), was evaluated from the GM.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 2.2. Electrochemical analyses
text: A potential difference, Δ η, defined by Δ η = η (average at 100 rpm)  (average at 1000 rpm), was evaluated from the GM. This value is a good indicator offilling performance [17,22,23]. Ifthe value is positive, it means that strong convection results in less copper deposition; thus, the plating solution may be effective for bottom-up filling (BUF) of microvia, whereas it is ineffective for BUF when the Δ η value is zero or negative. This approach was also adopted for this study to characterize the electrochemical behavior of these additives, providing further information for the BUF mechanism.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 2.3. Measurements of physical properties of copper deposits
text: The surface morphologies of the copper deposits formed from different plating solutions were examined by a scanning electron microscope (SEM) (Hitachi S-3500N). Before the SEM examination, a possible copper oxide existing on the samples was removed by immersion in a diluted sulfuric acid solution. The structure orientation of the copper deposits was examined by X-ray diffraction (XRD) (MXP3, MAC SCIENCE) using Cu K_α1 radiation ( λ = 1.5 4 0 5 A).

text: The structure orientation of the copper deposits was examined by X-ray diffraction (XRD) (MXP3, MAC SCIENCE) using Cu K_α1 radiation ( λ = 1.5 4 0 5 A). The etching rate ofthe copper deposits was obtained by measur ing the weight loss of a copper foil ( 3 cm × 5 cm) after immersing the copper foil in an etching solution that was composed of4% ( v / v) H _ 2 O _ 2 and 1 0 % ( v/v) H _ 2 S 0 _ 4. The temperature ofthe etching solution was maintained at 2 8 ^ ° C. The copper foil with a thickness of 50 -m was formed by plating on a stainless steel plate using the required copper plating formula.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 2.3. Measurements of physical properties of copper deposits
text: The copper foil with a thickness of 50 -m was formed by plating on a stainless steel plate using the required copper plating formula. It was then peeled off from the stainless steel plate. The etching solution contacted only one side ofthe copper foil that did not attach the surface of the stainless steel plate. The other side of the copper foil that was directly attached to the surface of the stainless steel plate was stuck tightly with tape to prevent corrosion. The etching time was 60 min. Each etching rate was measured three times to minimize the possibility of error.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.1. Effect ofDB addition onfilling performance
text: Fig. 1 shows the molecular structures of DB and JGB. They are very similar, except for that DB has a functional alcohol group. Alcohol may be oxidized by H_2 SO _4 or by anodic current to be a carboxyl group, which forms a chelating complex with metallic ions and has the ability to form hydrogen bonds with each other or with H_2 O. Hence, small amounts of precipitate always appear in the plating solution after electroplating. Table 1 lists the plating results obtained from various plating formulas, showing that only two formulas resulted in BUF of microvia.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.1. Effect ofDB addition onfilling performance
text: Table 1 lists the plating results obtained from various plating formulas, showing that only two formulas resulted in BUF of microvia. One formula had 0.3 ppm SPS and no DB, and the other formula had 1 ppm SPS and 1 ppm DB. The rest of these formulas did not led to BUF but to conformal deposition. PEG–Cl is a well-known suppressor, and SPS–Cl has been confirmed to be an accelerator for copper electrodeposition [5,7,8,10,26–52].

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.1. Effect ofDB addition onfilling performance
text: PEG–Cl is a well-known suppressor, and SPS–Cl has been confirmed to be an accelerator for copper electrodeposition [5,7,8,10,26–52]. Hence, the results listed in Table 1 indicate that the BUF behavior is caused by a synergistic interaction between the suppressor and the accelerator and that when the accelerator concentration is high, a leveler is an indispensable additive for achieving BUF.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.1. Effect ofDB addition onfilling performance
text: The SPS concentration must be low for the BUF of microvia when DB is absent in the plating solution. Considering the function of SPS–Cl, the failure in the microvia filling caused by the high SPS concentration is attributable to the loss of synergy between suppression and acceleration; that is, the ratio of acceleration to inhibition is too high to effectively inhibit copper deposition on the board surface. This is also the reason why the surface appearance of the copper deposit is not bright and smooth but matte and rough.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.2. Electrochemical behavior ofthe additives
text: Fig. 3 shows potential variations in galvanostatic measurements on a Cu-RDE at two rotating speeds. The individual additive was injected into the base electrolyte in sequence. Fig. 3A shows that DB interacts with chloride ions to be a depolarizer for copper deposition. This electrochemical behavior is different from that of JGB, which exhibits a slight inhibition of copper deposition in the presence of chloride ions [16,18].

The deposition rate was Cu(II) diffusion-controlled before PEG was added in the plating solution because the cathodic potential decreased as the rotating speed increased ( i. e., Δ η < 0). After PEG was injected into the plating solution, the cathodic potential suddenly dropped by a wide margin, and the value of- equaled zero.

The depolarization behavior proceeding with the plating time was immediately suppressed by adding DB, as recorded by curves (c)–(f) of Fig.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.3. Effect ofDB concentration onfilling performance
text: The depolarization behavior proceeding with the plating time was immediately suppressed by adding DB, as recorded by curves (c)–(f) of Fig. 6, indicating that the steady-state cathodic potentials were immediately shifted from the range of approximately 0.55 to 0.56 V to the range of approximately 0.6 to about 0.64 V. In addition, an  wave that represents a transient surface composition change, which varies from an accelerator-dominated composition to a leveler-dominated one, appears in Fig. 6. The transient time depends on the DB concentration and the strength of convection.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.3. Effect ofDB concentration onfilling performance
text: The transient time depends on the DB concentration and the strength of convection. A higher DB concentration or a stronger forced convection leads to a shorter transient time. Moffat et al. [53] proposed a model to explain the competitive adsorption between an accelerator and a leveler and simulated similar transient curves during plating.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.4. Influence ofthe additives on physical properties ofcopper deposit
text: The influence ofthe additives on the surface morphology ofcopper deposit was observed using SEM. Fig. 7 shows the top views of the copper deposits obtained from different plating formulas. Only two formulas, namely, PEG + Cl ^- + SPS and PEG + Cl− + SPS + DB, led to a flat plane within a micron range, as shown in Fig. 7e and f. Particularly, only the formula with PEG + Cl− + SPS + DB resulted in an overall mirror-like surface. The other formulas resulted in a marked micron roughness on the copper deposits. In the absence of SPS, the copper deposit had a small crystal size, as shown in Fig. 7d.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.4. Influence ofthe additives on physical properties ofcopper deposit
text: In the absence of SPS, the copper deposit had a small crystal size, as shown in Fig. 7d. The largest copper crystal size was obtained from the plating solution containing SPS only, as shown in Fig. 7b. In addition, the plating formula composed of PEG, Cl−, and SPS could not give rise to a macro flatness of copper deposit, as shown in Fig. 2c and d, but only resulted in a local flatness within a range in micron scale, as shown in Fig. 7e.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.4. Influence ofthe additives on physical properties ofcopper deposit
text: 2c and d, but only resulted in a local flatness within a range in micron scale, as shown in Fig. 7e. These results give us an insight into the interaction of these additives, which shows that DB, a nominal leveler, cannot flatten the surface of the copper deposit by itself, and SPS, a nominal brightener, cannot brighten the surface of the copper deposit. The mirror-like copper surface results from the interaction of these additives, which causes an equal copper growth rate in the vertical and horizontal directions.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.4. Influence ofthe additives on physical properties ofcopper deposit
text: The surface flatness of the copper deposit caused by the participation of DB in the plating formula with multiple components did not vary with the increase in the DB concentration until the DB concentration was higher than 15 ppm. These results were demonstrated by the SEM images, as shown in Fig. 8. As can be seen from Fig. 8, as the DB concentration increased, the surface flatness of the copper deposit was maintained until the DB concentration increased to 16 ppm.

text: 8, as the DB concentration increased, the surface flatness of the copper deposit was maintained until the DB concentration increased to 16 ppm. The plating formula that contained a DB concentration higher than 10 ppm would forfeit the synergistic effect on forming a mirror-like surface, implying that a high concentration of DB dominated the surface composition on the plated copper, resulting in an SEM image similar to that shown in Fig. 7a. The crystalline orientation ofthe copper deposits was characterized by XRD, as plotted in Fig. 9.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.4. Influence ofthe additives on physical properties ofcopper deposit
text: The crystalline orientation ofthe copper deposits was characterized by XRD, as plotted in Fig. 9. Not only the surface morphology but also the crystalline orientation was subject to the addition of DB. The intensity of[1 1 1] and [2 0 0] orientation peaks significantly decreased after DB was added in the plating solution. On the other hand, the intensity of [2 2 0] orientation peak obviously increased due to the addition of DB. A similar result was also found in other copper plating systems [54–56]. Honma et al.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.4. Influence ofthe additives on physical properties ofcopper deposit
text: A similar result was also found in other copper plating systems [54–56]. Honma et al. [54] reported that the addition of a leveler in a plating bath causes the [2 2 0] orientation to be dominant. After annealing at 120 ◦C for 1 h, the [1 1 1] orientation rather than the [2 2 0] orientation becomes dominant [54]. The change in the preferential orientation will lead to a change in the chemical activity of the surface copper atoms, which can be characterized by an etching test.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.4. Influence ofthe additives on physical properties ofcopper deposit
text: As can be seen from Fig. 10, the etching rate ofthe copper deposit decreased with an increased DB concentration in the plating solution. However, when the DB concentration was higher than 4 ppm, the etching rate did not vary with the DB concentration. The results are attributable to the difference in the atomic densities ofdifferent orientation and to the change in the preferential orientation ofthese copper films caused by DB addition. The grain size of [2 2 0], which was determined using Scherrer equation [57,58], also decreased with the DB concentration.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.4. Influence ofthe additives on physical properties ofcopper deposit
text: The grain size of [2 2 0], which was determined using Scherrer equation [57,58], also decreased with the DB concentration. A significant drop occurred at 1 ppm DB, indicating that DB is refining agent, that can lead to fine grains. Hence, the appearance ofthe copper film looked like a mirror when DB was present in the plating bath mixed with PEG, SPS, and chlo-

text: ride ions. However, the etching rate is dominated by the [1 1 1] orientation because of its high atomic density. Therefore, when the preferential orientation changed from [1 1 1] to [2 2 0], the etching rate correspondingly declined as well.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 4. Conclusions
text: A leveler, namely DB, employed for microvia filling was tested in this study. An excellent filling performance is obtained from a copper plating formula composed of 200 ppm PEG, 60 ppm Cl−, 1 ppm SPS, and 1 ppm DB. This plating formula not only results in BUF of microvias but also leads to a mirror-like copper surface. According to electrochemical analyses, the root cause for achieving BUF in the plating solution was attributed to the CDA behavior ofthis formula. Although DB is a derivative of JGB, their electrochemical behaviors are somewhat different.

section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 4. Conclusions
text: Although DB is a derivative of JGB, their electrochemical behaviors are somewhat different. DB cannot enhance the suppression of PEG–Cl on copper deposition, whereas JGB can do that. Nevertheless, DB can effectively suppress the acceleration of SPS–Cl on copper deposition in the presence of PEG. The preferential orientation of the plated copper films is changed from [1 1 1] to [2 2 0] because of the addition of DB, which causes a decrease in the etching rate of the plated copper film and results in fine grains and mirror-like copper surfaces.
